2023 · arXiv · Benchmarks & Evals

EQ-Bench: An Emotional Intelligence Benchmark for Large Language Models

A 60-question benchmark that asks a model to rate the intensity of four emotions felt by a character in a GPT-4-written dialogue of conflict, then scores the answer by its distance from author-chosen reference ratings -- not right/wrong. The single-author result: scores span a wide range (GPT-4-0613 at 62.52 down to a failing OpenAI Babbage) and correlate with MMLU at r=0.97.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

By late 2023 the standard ways of scoring an LLM fell into three buckets: multi-domain multiple-choice question-answering, LLM-as-a-judge, and ranking by human preference of output. The paper spells out drawbacks for the first two -- multi-domain QA suites like MMLU need thousands of questions (14,079 for MMLU alone) to cover broad knowledge and are easy to game by targeting a model's training data on the specific domains covered, and LLM-as-a-judge scores (AlpacaEval-style) inherit the judge model's own biases, with the paper quoting AlpacaEval's own warning that "GPT-4 may favor models with longer outputs and/or those that were fine-tuned on GPT-4 outputs" -- but doesn't spell out a specific drawback for the third, human-preference ranking (e.g. Chatbot Arena). None of the three specifically targets emotional understanding (EU) -- the ability to interpret complex emotions and social context in language -- despite EU being central to how people actually judge a model's perceived intelligence in conversation.

The one existing EU-specific test, SECEU (Wang et al., 2023), is closer in spirit: it shows a short scenario and asks the model to rate the relative strength of four candidate emotions. But the paper argues SECEU has four concrete defects. First, its reference answers are the average of a human cohort's own ratings, which the author argues compresses the test's usable range toward the human mean -- evidenced by SECEU scoring OpenAI's Babbage and Curie models at or above the human average, and placing the 13B-parameter Curie within 2.6% of the far larger GPT-3.5-turbo. Second, its scenarios are short descriptions without dialogue, giving less to reason about. Third, SECEU requires the four intensity ratings to sum to exactly 10, which the paper argues both taxes models' arithmetic (citing Hendrycks et al.'s MATH benchmark on LLMs' struggles with basic math) and forces sequential dependence -- because LLMs generate token-by-token, earlier ratings constrain how many points are left for later ones. Fourth, SECEU picks the four "most plausible" emotions for a scenario, which the paper argues narrows the ambiguity the test is meant to probe. EQ-Bench is pitched as a fix for all four: author-chosen (not crowd-averaged) references, richer GPT-4-generated conflict dialogues, ratings that don't have to sum to anything, and a deliberately more diverse (not just "most plausible") set of four emotions per question.

// how it works

The method

Each of the benchmark's 60 questions presents a short GPT-4-generated dialogue depicting a scene of conflict or tension (the author found that without this "conflict" constraint, GPT-4 tended to generate dialogue that resolved too predictably to carry emotional nuance). The model is then asked to rate, on a 0-10 intensity scale, how strongly one named character would be feeling each of four listed emotions -- typically a mix of options that are clearly wrong, obvious, or require a nuanced understanding of the scene to rate accurately. Questions are administered zero-shot, and the model is prompted to give first-pass scores, write a step-by-step critique of its own answer, and then give revised scores -- both the first-pass and revised answers are kept and scored separately.

Scoring has three steps. First, the model's four raw ratings are normalized to sum to 10 (the reference answers are already stored pre-normalized this way) -- this deliberately shifts what's being measured from "how intense is this emotion in absolute terms" to "how does the model rank the relative intensity of the four emotions," sidestepping the kind of absolute-intensity subjectivity the paper compares to self-reported pain scales in medicine. Second, the sum of the absolute differences between the model's normalized ratings and the normalized reference ratings is computed. Third, that sum is subtracted from a constant of 10 to produce the question's score -- the constant is chosen specifically so that answering completely at random averages out to a score of 0.

score = 10 − Σ|normalized rating − normalized reference| // worked example from the paper: subject ratings 6,0,7,7 → normalized to 3,0,3.5,3.5; reference (pre-normalized) 1,0,4,5; score = 10 − (|3−1|+|0−0|+|3.5−4|+|3.5−5|) = 10 − 4 = 6

A model's final EQ-Bench score is the mean of its per-question scores across only the questions it answered in a parsable format -- unparsable answers are excluded rather than scored zero, so the benchmark isn't conflating emotional understanding with output-formatting compliance. If fewer than 50 of the 60 questions come back parsable, the run is marked a FAIL rather than given a low numeric score. In practice most models produced close to 60 parsable answers; only three legacy OpenAI completion models (Babbage, ADA, Curie) struggled with the format under the standard protocol, and all three initially failed the 50-answer threshold -- Curie and ADA's Table 1 scores (9.28 and 2.25) were only obtained by simplifying the prompt to remove the critique-and-revision section, and even then the paper notes both scores are close to what random answering would produce; Babbage is the one model Table 1 records as an outright FAIL. A model's reported benchmark score is the better of its two scores -- first-pass and post-critique revised, both drawn from this single administration of the 60 questions, not two independent runs -- rather than the best answer per question, which the author notes would disproportionately reward wild guessing on individual questions. Open-source models were run quantized via bitsandbytes -- 8-bit for 7B-34B parameter models, 4-bit above that -- which the author flags as a possible source of score suppression for those models specifically.

// what they found

The results

Across the 25 models/checkpoints in Table 1, EQ-Bench scores spread from a high of 62.52 (OpenAI's gpt-4-0613, the top score "by a considerable margin," per the paper) down to a FAIL for OpenAI's Babbage; the lowest passing score was 2.25 (OpenAI ADA). The best open-source model was SynthIA-70B-v1.5, a Llama-2-70B fine-tune built for role-play, at 54.83 -- ahead of gpt-4-0314 (53.39), Qwen-72B-Chat (52.44), Anthropic's Claude 2 (52.14), and Llama-2-70b-chat (51.56). The paper reads this as open models "rapidly closing the gap" with proprietary frontier models on this axis, and notes newer GPT-3.5/GPT-4 checkpoints scoring above their older siblings.

Repeatability was measured over multiple runs per model with an average coefficient of variation of 2.93%, which the paper attributes to ordinary LLM output non-determinism rather than a flaw in the test design. Prompting the model to critique and revise its own first-pass answer raised scores by 9.3% on average, though the benefit was uneven: weaker models tended to gain more, and for some models (e.g. mistral-openorca-7b, qwen-14b) the revised pass scored consistently lower than the first pass across the repeated runs in Appendix E.

The paper's central evidence is a correlation analysis against six established benchmarks, computed as Pearson's r over the subset of models it could evaluate on both sides: MMLU r=0.97 (paired over 16 models), Arena ELO (Chatbot Arena) r=0.94, HellaSwag r=0.91, MT-Bench r=0.91, AlpacaEval r=0.91, and ARC r=0.85. Two comparisons came back markedly weaker: TruthfulQA at r=0.44 and SECEU EQ at r=0.22 (paired over just 8 models; the AlpacaEval panel is thinner still at 7 — Table 3 shows eight rows carrying both scores, but the printed 0.91 only reproduces over seven of them, and rises from 0.80 if Mistral-7B-Instruct is included, whose AlpacaEval cell of 54.52 is the same number as its ARC cell) -- the paper explicitly separates these out as the "weaker correlations." Because EQ-Bench and SECEU use a similar rate-four-emotions format but disagree with each other far more than either agrees with MMLU/Arena-ELO/MT-Bench, the paper argues its four methodological changes (dialogue-based scenarios, author-chosen references, no forced sum-to-10, more diverse emotion sets) are what's driving the difference, and separately reports that normalized EQ-Bench scores have a wider interquartile range (53.81 vs. SECEU's 14.71) and are closer to symmetric (skewness 0.13 vs. SECEU's -0.68) -- i.e. EQ-Bench spreads the 9 models common to both benchmarks out more and bunches them less than SECEU does over the same normalized 0-100 scale.

The paper also highlights one specific parameter-scaling comparison as evidence that EQ-Bench is more sensitive than an aggregate of standard benchmarks: on an aggregate of ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU and TruthfulQA, Meta's 70B Llama-2-chat model scores only 1.4% higher than the 7B Mistral-OpenOrca fine-tune, whereas EQ-Bench scores the 70B model 13.9% higher than the 7B one.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

The headline correlation numbers are real and the methodology section is unusually candid about the test's own limitations, but the benchmark's foundations are narrower than the correlation table alone suggests. All 60 questions are drawn from one format (a GPT-4-written conflict dialogue, four emotions, 0-10 ratings) and every reference answer was set by the sole author's own judgment call, not by any external rater, expert panel, or human cohort -- the paper says as much directly ("all questions and reference answers were determined by the authors of this paper"). That's a defensible design choice against SECEU's crowd-averaging problem, but it swaps one source of bias (compression toward a human mean) for another (one person's intuitions about what a fictional character "should" feel), and the paper offers no inter-rater or expert-validation check on those reference answers at all -- a point the Limitations section itself concedes, alongside acknowledging that no human baseline was administered to anchor the 0-100 scale to anything outside the model comparison itself.

The correlation evidence, while strong, rests on a small and uneven model pool: Figure 5's panels range from n=9 (SECEU EQ, the weakest correlation) up to n=16 (MMLU, the strongest) -- an r of 0.97 is a different claim at 16 paired models than it would be at 60 -- and several benchmarks, like Arena ELO or AlpacaEval, have gaps for models where no public score existed at the time. The models compared also span wildly different capability tiers: the lowest points actually plotted are legacy models like Oasst-pythia-12B (7.69) and text-davinci-001 (15.19), with text-curie-001 (13.55) appearing only in the SECEU panel and neither Ada nor Babbage scoring well enough to appear in any correlation panel at all, up to GPT-4 at the top of the range. A regression line fit across such a wide capability spread will tend to look strong almost regardless of what's being measured, because "how good is this model overall" is itself highly correlated with everything else in that spread; the paper doesn't test whether the correlation holds up within a narrower band of similarly-capable contemporary models, which is the harder and more useful question for a benchmark meant to discriminate between current frontier systems. It also can't rule out training-data leakage: dialogues are GPT-4-generated but the reference answers and question format have been public (via the GitHub repo and eqbench.com leaderboard) since the paper's release, and the paper's own "Difficult to Game" section acknowledges this is a real, unaddressed risk it intends only to "monitor," not to have already tested for.

One internal wrinkle worth flagging at its real size rather than softened: the appendix correlation-matrix tables (Tables 3-5) list different EQ-Bench scores than Table 1 for at least six shared checkpoints, and the gaps are not uniformly small. gpt-4-0613 drifts only 0.42 points (62.52 in Table 1 vs. 62.94 in Tables 3 and 4), but gpt-4-0314 drifts 7.34 points -- 53.39 in Table 1 versus 60.73 in Tables 3-5 -- a gap large enough that, taken at face value, it would place gpt-4-0314 second overall, ahead of the paper's own "best open model," SynthIA-70B-v1.5 (54.83). gpt-3.5-turbo-0301 (47.61 vs. 49.52) and Llama-2-13b-chat (33.02 vs. 32.34) show smaller drift, and text-davinci-002/003 appear to have their two values swapped between tables entirely (Table 1: 002=39.44, 003=43.73; Tables 3-5: 002=43.73, 003=39.44), as does Curie, listed as 9.28 in Table 1 but 13.55 as "text-curie-001" in Table 5. Most likely this reflects a separate benchmark run collected for the correlation study, but the paper never says so explicitly or reconciles the two sets of numbers, so a reader comparing tables directly should treat neither one as the single canonical score for these checkpoints -- this isn't evidence the paper's headline claims are wrong, but it does mean the exact ranking of several mid-table models shouldn't be taken as fixed.

baselines

The four GPT-4/GPT-3.5 checkpoints and Claude 2 anchor the top of the range, but most of the 25-model panel is already a generation or more behind by any 2023 standard, and open-weight coverage stops at 70B-class models -- there's no frontier-scale open model (e.g. nothing near GPT-4's scale) to test whether the discriminative power holds at the very top.

contamination

Not tested. The paper flags training-set leakage as a known, unaddressed risk for any public benchmark and explicitly defers investigating it to "future research"; nothing in this paper measures whether any tested model had prior exposure to the released question set.

what's missed

A single author's subjective reference answers stand in for ground truth with no external validation (no expert panel, no human cohort, no inter-rater check); the correlation analysis spans models of very different eras and capability tiers rather than testing discrimination within a tight capability band.

would raise confidence

An independent expert or crowd-validated check on the reference answers; a correlation study restricted to contemporaneous, similarly-capable models; and a documented contamination check on the public question set now that it has been live since December 2023.

// bottom line

EQ-Bench is a clever, cheap (well under an hour of compute per model), and genuinely discriminating diagnostic that improves on SECEU's design in every way it claims to -- but its correlation with broad-capability benchmarks is also its main limitation as an emotional-intelligence measure specifically: a test whose scores track MMLU at r=0.97 is arguably still measuring general model capability more than any distinct construct of emotional understanding, a tension the paper itself raises but doesn't fully resolve.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. EQ-Bench scores 60 GPT-4-generated conflict dialogues by asking a model to rate four emotions' intensity (0-10), normalizing both the model's and the reference's ratings to sum to 10, then scoring each question as 10 minus the summed absolute difference -- a relative-ranking metric, not an accuracy metric, calibrated so random answers average to 0.
  2. GPT-4-0613 scored highest at 62.52; the best open model was SynthIA-70B-v1.5 (a role-play fine-tune of Llama-2-70B) at 54.83; three legacy OpenAI completion models (Babbage, ADA, Curie) sat at the bottom, with Babbage failing to produce enough parsable answers to score at all.
  3. The paper's strongest evidence is a correlation table: EQ-Bench correlates with MMLU at r=0.97, Chatbot Arena ELO at r=0.94, and HellaSwag/MT-Bench/AlpacaEval all around r=0.91 -- but correlates only weakly with SECEU (r=0.22), the one other EU-specific benchmark it's explicitly built to improve on.
